sites.name: au-ip
sites.description: Every patent, trade mark, registered design and plant breeder's right ever filed in Australia — 4,332,386 applications from 1904 to 2026, read out of IP Australia's IP RAPID release. The register is public but ships as ONE 1.33 GB ZIP that expands to 9.51 GB across six CSVs with no per-table download, which is why nobody reads it; the pipeline reads the Zip64 central directory over HTTP range requests and raw-inflates only the three members it needs (application.csv, party_activity.csv, application_classification.csv), aggregating line-by-line in constant memory — the 4.2 GB events table is never touched and the 9.51 GB never hits disk, so a full refresh is ~95s. Built around one finding nothing public shows, because it needs Australian-origin filing separated from foreign filing INTO Australia: Australian-origin patent filings FELL in absolute terms, 8,897 (1995) to 6,569 (2023), while foreign filings grew 2.4x — yet 58.0% of trade mark applications are still Australian against 18.3% of patents. Australia registers the world's brands and has largely stopped patenting its own inventions. Secondary findings: Australia over-indexes in civil engineering (+8.4pp) and furniture & games (+4.7pp, i.e. gaming machines) and under-indexes hardest in pharmaceuticals (-6.2pp); CSIRO is the most prolific Australian filer (7,591 founding-applicant filings, ahead of Aristocrat's 6,896 once its four registered-name variants merge); the innovation patent's abolition on 26 Aug 2021 is visible as a legislative cliff. Nine views, deliberately not the house stack: Divergence (mirrored area small-multiples, Australian above the axis and foreign below, because a stacked chart hides that the two series move in OPPOSITE directions), Origin (Leaflet world choropleth on Natural Earth, LOG ramp because the US alone out-files the next twenty countries), Technology (WIPO-35 field x decade heatmap on a LINEAR row-relative ramp + a DIVERGING specialisation bar, the only form that can express under-indexing), Filers (merged filer groups with the merge rule inspectable — every drill-down lists the registered names combined), Attorneys (radial hub-and-spoke of the applicant-to-attorney-firm relation from 3.8M agent rows, published nowhere else; analytic layout so it is motionless from the first frame and cannot overlap), Lifecycle (grant-lag CDFs + right-censored survival curves + the innovation-patent cliff), Brands (squarified treemap of all 45 Nice classes split by origin), States (per-capita choropleth on a LINEAR ramp — raw counts just redraw the population map), Overview. Honesty is load-bearing: each divergence panel STARTS in a different year (patents 1988, trade marks 1958, designs 1981) because the applicant-country field was back-filled and 87% of 1980 patents have no recorded country, so charting them draws the field being populated rather than filings being made; share figures stop at 2023 for PCT national-phase lag; 538,824 applicant and 443,758 agent records are pseudonymised at source and excluded from every ranking with the volume disclosed per firm. Eight reconciliation gates, the load-bearing one anchored to the SOURCE row count after the original proved a tautology that stayed green while silently dropping all 11,649 plant breeder's rights (the type is 'pbr', not the guessed 'plant_breeders_right'). A 39-agent adversarial pre-deploy review produced 35 findings, each independently verified by an agent told to refute it: 16 refuted, 19 confirmed and all 19 fixed — including a critical one where the attorney client map published a company that does not exist, because every pseudonymised applicant collapsed into one client that took whichever raw name it saw first and rendered as the largest client of 37 of 60 firms. Genuinely new domain: nothing in the fleet touched intellectual property, and IP Australia is a new publisher for the factory. Monthly cron (source is weekly). IP RAPID CC BY 4.0; ABS boundaries + ERP CC BY 4.0; Natural Earth public domain.

sites.name: au-towers
sites.description: Every mobile base station Telstra, Optus and TPG operate in Australia — 25,930 sites in the 2025 snapshot (Telstra 11,644 / Optus 9,172 / TPG 5,114), from the ACCC's mandatory Audit of Telecommunications Infrastructure Assets returns, 2018–2025, ~205,000 site-year rows across 25 CSVs. Organised around the fact carriers never advertise: a tower's REACH is set by its frequencies, not its generation label — sub-1 GHz (700/850/900 MHz) carries tens of kilometres across country, 1.8–3.6 GHz does not, so a '5G tower' running only NR3600 reaches nobody new. Headline findings, all pipeline-computed with the rule shown on hover: (1) across 61.6% of Australia's LAND AREA exactly one carrier holds meaningful long-reach spectrum (23 of 340 SA3s, Telstra in 21 of the populated ones, ~600,781 people) — the map's colour is a categorical carrier-SET encoding, not a magnitude ramp, so it answers 'do I get a choice' rather than 'how many towers'; (2) 455 of the 2,161 measurable co-funded towers (21%) sit within 50 m of a COMPETING carrier's tower and 142 share exact coordinates — i.e. the same mast, where a signal already reached; (3) Telstra holds 66.5% of publicly co-funded sites while running 42.9% of commercially built ones, a capture ratio of 1.55x against Optus 0.72x and TPG 0.35x, and its slope runs UP in every jurisdiction; (4) 3G collapsed 22,194 → 158 sites in two years with TPG a full year ahead, and 877 individual towers held long-reach 3G then ended with NO sub-1 GHz spectrum at all — still standing, physically shorter reach; (5) the money did broadly follow need — 23.6% of towers in the thinnest-covered quarter of regional Australia are publicly funded vs 6.2% in the best-covered. Nine views, deliberately NOT the house stack (exactly ONE choropleth, ZERO ranked-bar charts, no treemap): Coverage (Leaflet categorical carrier-set map on real ABS SA3 boundaries + 25,930 individual towers at zoom>=9, MOCN toggle re-crediting TPG for 2,442 shared Optus sites); My Address (point-level ruler — distance from a chosen point to each carrier's nearest tower AND its nearest LONG-REACH tower, the gap between them being 'there is a tower' vs 'it can reach me', with a plain-English verdict); Spectrum (the signature view — a frequency LADDER whose vertical axis is true centre frequency in MHz so each carrier's reach-vs-capacity silhouette is legible, and the bands a carrier doesn't use are visible holes: Telstra WCDMA/NR2600/NR3600 vs Optus UMTS/NR2300/NR3500 vs TPG NR1800); Switch-Off (a six-column alluvial tracking individual towers by RFNSA site number through the 3G shutdown, amber ribbons = reach lost, click a ribbon to materialise the cohort); Public Money (co-funded towers binned by distance to the nearest RIVAL network, with 'same structure' as its own broken-axis category, click a bar for the tower list); Capture (slope small multiples per jurisdiction — the finding is a ratio near or far from 1, which a ranked bar cannot express); Targeting (quadrant scatter of 2018 tower density vs share publicly funded, restricted to non-capital regions); Regions (three-carrier verdict card reusing the frequency axis, so a shortfall reads as a hole at a named frequency); Overview (the 3G cliff + ten auto-detected findings). Genuinely new domain: nothing in the fleet covered telecommunications infrastructure, and no neutral cross-carrier tower map exists in Australia — carrier coverage maps are marketing artefacts and deliberately non-comparable, rfnsa.com.au is a per-site regulatory lookup. Dependency-free unit-tested pipeline (pipeline/parse.mjs shared with the tests) handling four real file traps: optus-2023.csv is cp1252 not UTF-8; telstra-2021-v2.csv carries 20 rows with impossible Year values 2022–2041; the 2018/2019 files have NO site identifier so per-tower history can only start in 2020; and ~3,100 rows across all years are separate installations sharing one registered site number, merged by OR-ing band flags. Seven gates, the load-bearing one anchored to the SOURCE files (every data row in all 25 CSVs must be accepted or in a named rejection bucket) — added after a pre-deploy review proved the original six were tautologies by deleting 601 real towers with all six still green. Annual cron matching the ACCC's annual publication. ACCC data CC BY 2.5 AU; ABS boundaries + ERP CC BY 4.0; attribution in the footer and About panel.

sites.name: au-warming
sites.description: Australia's official homogenised temperature record — the Bureau of Meteorology's ACORN-SAT (Australian Climate Observations Reference Network – Surface Air Temperature) for all 112 long-record reference stations, daily 1910→2024 — turned into one explorer built around the single fact the raw text files bury: Australia's average temperature has risen about 1.46 °C since 1910 (a 0.13 °C/decade trend that matches the Bureau's own State of the Climate figure of ~1.5 °C), 2024 was the hottest year on record (+1.4 °C vs 1961–1990), overnight lows are warming FASTER than daytime highs (nights +0.14 vs days +0.11 °C/decade), 35 °C+ days are up ~38% (36→49 a year at the average station) and frost nights are down (21→17), and warming is near-universal — only 2 of 112 stations sit below 0.06 °C/decade (West Wyalong NSW fastest at +0.29). The signature view is the #ShowYourStripes idiom: the national annual mean-temperature anomaly rendered as a blue→red stripe banner plus a small-multiple grid of every station's stripes (sortable by rate/name/state, filterable by state) that literally goes from blue to red down each row. Nine views: Overview (the +1.5 °C hero, the national stripe banner + legend, a year-by-year anomaly line with an OLS trend line and hottest-year marker, six stat tiles, and a fastest-warming leaderboard); Stripes (the per-station small-multiple grid); Map (a Leaflet light-basemap with all 112 stations as circle markers over faint real ABS state polygons — in their OWN lower pane so they never cover the markers — coloured by four modes: warming rate / recent-decade anomaly / nights-minus-days / hot-day trend, click a marker → station drawer painting above Leaflet); Nights vs Days (a dual national anomaly line + a per-station day-rate-vs-night-rate scatter with a y=x 'equal warming' diagonal and zoom/pan — most points sit on the nights-faster side); Hot & Cold (35 °C+ days and frost nights per year, national or per selected station, + biggest-riser/biggest-frost-loss leaderboards); Seasons (a per-station month×year anomaly heatmap that reddens downward + a client-side-computed per-season warming bar chart — summer vs winter); Rankings (five leaderboards — fastest warming, hottest recently, nights warming, most hot days, losing frosts fastest, colour-coded vs the median — + a squarified station treemap sized by total warming, shaded by rate, with zoom/pan); Explorer (a searchable/sortable table of all 112 stations with anomaly sparklines + a click-to-filter warming-rate histogram + per-station drawer); and Insights (8 auto-detected findings). Plus hash-linkable per-station drawers (#s=086338) with 8 stat tiles (rate, total warming, night/day rates, recent anomaly, hot days, record high & low with dates — e.g. Melbourne's 45.9 °C on Black Saturday 7 Feb 2009), the station's stripes, and a lazily-loaded month×year heatmap; a full glossary of ℹ popovers (ACORN-SAT, anomaly, baseline, homogenisation, rate, tmax/tmin, hot day, frost…) and an honest About modal that foregrounds the 1961–1990 baseline, the homogenisation caveat, and that the national figure is a simple station mean not the Bureau's area-weighted gridding. Deliberately light warm-paper civic theme (not a terminal) with a SINGLE cool-blue→warm-red diverging anomaly ramp used identically across every view so colour always means cooler/warmer-than-normal. Dependency-free unit-tested pipeline (its own daily-CSV reader + daily→monthly→annual aggregator + anomaly/trend/hot-day maths + point-in-polygon state tagging in pipeline/parse.mjs, shared with 52 vitest tests) with THREE reconciliation gates so a bad parse can't ship: (1) a two-way annual-mean cross-check — each station-year's mean computed directly from daily values must equal the day-weighted mean of its 12 monthly means to 0.01 °C (9,940 checks, 0 fails, worst 0 °C); (2) a raw-value sanity range (tmax −20..55, tmin −30..45); and (3) a national-trend ANCHOR gate — the computed national warming must land in the Bureau's published range (rate 0.13 ∈ [0.08, 0.20] °C/decade AND total 1.46 ∈ [1.0, 2.0] °C), so a scale/column error throws it out of range. Traps handled: a month needs ≥20 valid days and a year needs all 12 valid months to count; anomalies need ≥20 valid 1961–1990 baseline years (a few post-1970 stations like Learmonth are shown in the Explorer with absolute rates but omitted from stripes and the national mean); the current daily files live at /climate/change/hqsites/data/temp/ (the easy /change/acorn/sat/ URL is the stale 2017 v2.1 release); homogenised record extremes differ slightly from raw and this is stated. Annual data pipeline (BOM refreshes ACORN-SAT once a year ~Feb–Mar — the slowest proportional cadence the factory allows); embeds the latest DATA year (2024), not a run timestamp, so re-runs are idempotent (the CI Data Pipeline re-run produced NO commit). Genuinely new domain for the catalog: nothing else covers climate, long-term temperature or weather (au-dams is water storage, aurora-australis is space weather, quakewatch is geohazards). ACORN-SAT + ABS boundaries are © Commonwealth of Australia, CC BY 4.0; attribution preserved in the About panel + footer.

sites.name: quakewatch
sites.description: A live global earthquake monitor — every earthquake on Earth right now, turned from the USGS Earthquake Hazards Program's raw real-time feed into one plain-language dashboard that answers the only question most people have when the ground moves: was that an earthquake, how big, how deep, and am I in danger? Realtime and ENTIRELY client-side (the NEMWatch/DSN-Watch/aurora-australis class): the browser fetches the public, keyless, CORS-enabled USGS summary GeoJSON feed directly and re-polls every 60s while the tab is visible, with a visible 'updated Xs ago' stamp — NO server, NO scheduled Actions (the only workflow is the push-triggered deploy). The point is the interpretation layer USGS's own map lacks: it turns each event's magnitude into a felt/damage verdict and a TNT/energy comparison (log10(E)=1.5M+4.8), decodes depth and PAGER impact alerts, and — via in-browser point-in-polygon against the vendored Peter Bird (2003) PB2002 plate polygons — classifies every quake to the tectonic plate it sits on. Eight tab-views: Overview (a '211 earthquakes in the past day' hero with the largest event's plain-language verdict, six stat tiles incl. total seismic energy and the counter-intuitive energy-concentration % showing one quake dominates, a by-magnitude-class histogram, a most-active-plates leaderboard and a latest-events list); Live Map (a Leaflet dark basemap with the real tectonic plate boundaries as an overlay, every quake a marker sized by magnitude and coloured by depth with tsunami rings, hover tooltips, a plate-boundaries toggle, and click-to-drawer — the markers visibly trace the Ring of Fire along the plate lines); Magnitude (the signature Gutenberg–Richter view — a log-scale magnitude-frequency histogram + cumulative log-line + a live Aki-MLE b-value and magnitude of completeness, plus a squarified energy treemap where each tile is one quake sized by joules so the largest dwarf everything); Depth (a depth-distribution histogram + category donut + a zoom/pan magnitude-vs-depth scatter revealing the shallow-and-strong danger zone); Regions (a tectonic-plate leaderboard with a by-count/by-energy toggle + a region×magnitude-band cross-reference heatmap); Timeline (events per time-bucket coloured by max magnitude to reveal swarms/aftershock sequences + a cumulative-energy step line); Explorer (a searchable/sortable table of every event with region classification + a click-to-filter magnitude histogram + per-event drawer); and Insights (auto-detected findings — largest event, energy concentration, high-impact PAGER alerts, tsunami-zone events, most active plate, shallow share, b-value, felt reports, non-earthquake blasts). Plus hash-linkable per-event drawers (#event=us6000tgzc) with energy/TNT/depth/plate/felt/MMI/significance, a full glossary of ℹ popovers (moment magnitude, b-value, completeness, PAGER, MMI, tsunami flag, aftershock, swarm, Ring of Fire…) and an honest About modal that stresses the data is preliminary, coverage is denser where sensors are, and the tsunami flag is not an official warning. Deliberately dark-themed — a monitoring tool used at a glance, often at night; a fixed magnitude colour ramp (cyan→green→lime→yellow→orange→red→violet) and depth ramp (shallow-warm→deep-indigo) mean colour is consistent across every view. Dependency-free unit-tested model (the USGS GeoJSON parser robust to null-magnitude/non-Point/missing-id rows, the seismology maths — energy, magnitude/depth classes, Gutenberg–Richter binning + b-value, region classification, timeline bucketing — and positional SVG-layout maths, all in DOM-free modules shared with 49 vitest tests): parser tests incl. malformed-feed rejection and string-coercion, model tests incl. a synthetic GR distribution and the 31.6×-per-magnitude energy law, positional layout tests (histogram bars/scatter/grid/treemap: in-bounds, no overlap, flush, no-NaN, area-conserved) and a headless jsdom render of all 7 non-map views against a realistic fixture asserting no NaN/undefined/Infinity + each view's signature marks. Verified additionally by a live end-to-end check that fetched TODAY's real USGS feed through the exact compiled model (212 quakes parsed, all finite, largest M5.9, 100% classified to a plate, plausible region leaderboard — all assertions passed), the thing jsdom can't exercise. Genuinely new domain for the catalog: nothing else covers earthquakes, seismology or geohazards. USGS earthquake data is U.S. Government public domain; the PB2002 plate model + CARTO/OpenStreetMap basemap keep their own terms, credited in the About panel + footer.

sites.description: Forty-three years of the ABS Retail Trade release (dataflow RT, monthly Apr 1982 → Jun 2025) turned into one explorer built around the cost-of-living story of the decade: Australians now spend about $443.7bn a year at the shops (~$37.9bn a month), and while turnover keeps climbing in dollars (+3.3% year on year) the QUANTITY actually bought is nearly flat (+1.0% real chain volume) — most of the 'growth' in spending is inflation, not extra shopping. Second story: the shopping basket transformed — cafés, restaurants & takeaway ($66.3bn/yr) now dwarf department stores ($23.1bn/yr) by ~3×, food retailing anchors 40% of every retail dollar, and December towers over every other month. sites.name: au-births
sites.description: Fifty years of Australia's birth registrations (ABS, 1975–2024) turned into one explorer around a single fact: Australia is having fewer children, much later. Headline: the total fertility rate fell to a record-low 1.481 in 2024 (from 2.148 in 1975), below the 2.1 replacement rate where it has sat every year since 1976; the median age of mothers rose 25.8→32.1 (+6.3y, first-time mothers 30.8); teen (15–19) fertility collapsed 40.1→6.0 per 1,000 (−85%) while 35–39 fertility rose 26→66.6, now HIGHER than 20–24's 30.6 — women in their late 30s out-birth women in their early 20s; 39% of babies are now born outside marriage (up from 10% in 1975); NT has the highest fertility (1.629), ACT the lowest (1.273). The signature view is a hand-rolled age-of-mother fertility SURFACE — a warm heatmap of age-specific fertility rate by 5-year age group × year (7×50=350 cells) that shows the bright band of peak childbearing slide from the early-20s/25-29 to 30-34. Eight views: Overview (record-low hero, TFR line vs the 2.1 replacement reference with GST/GFC/COVID annotations, births bars, median-age lines); Fertility rate (national TFR + per-state multi-line + an above/below-replacement ranking); Older mothers (the ASFR surface with svg zoom/pan + a year-vs-1975 age-profile bar + median-age lines); By state (a real Leaflet ABS choropleth with 5 modes — fertility rate / crude birth rate / median mother age / ex-nuptial share / total births — and a click-through per-state drawer painting above Leaflet); Marriage (nuptial vs ex-nuptial stacked area share/number toggle + per-state ex-nuptial lines + median marriage-duration-at-birth); Seasonality (a year×month birth-calendar heatmap, complete years only through 2023 with the incomplete 2024 auto-excluded, + average month profile vs an even-8.3% line — March peak, February low); Explorer (every state-year in a sortable/searchable table + a click-to-filter TFR histogram); and Insights (9 auto-detected findings). Plus hash-linkable per-state drawers (#s=NSW), a full glossary of ℹ popovers and an honest About modal. Deliberately light civic palette (warm off-white, teal/coral) — it's about babies and families, not a terminal. Dependency-free unit-tested pipeline (its own ABS SDMX-JSON 2.0.0 reader + canonicalisers + three reconciliation gates in pipeline/parse.mjs, shared with 50 vitest tests) with THREE gates on INDEPENDENTLY-published ABS columns so agreement proves a correct parse: (1) cross-file EXACT — the two independent 'all births' columns (BIRTHS_SUMMARY vs FERTILITY_AGE_STATE all-ages) must agree (0.000% worst across 450 checks); (2) TFR demographic identity TOLERANT — published TFR must equal 5·Σ(5-yr ASFR)/1000 (1.14% worst); (3) nuptiality — nuptial+ex-nuptial must account for total births (3.96% worst, a legitimate Tasmanian 'not stated' residual 2007–2012; a shifted column produces 50%+ and still fails). Traps handled: maternal age not-stated (up to 7.5% in small states) excluded from the age breakdown but kept in totals — so the cross-file gate compares published all-ages totals, not the group sum; median marriage duration only exists under NUPT_STATUS=Nuptial; month-of-occurrence lags registration so the latest year's final months collapse (2024 Dec=0.18× median) and is auto-flagged incomplete by an internal min-month<50%-of-median test and dropped from seasonality. Annual data pipeline (ABS publishes Births, Australia once a year ~October — the slowest proportional cadence the factory allows); embeds the latest DATA year (2024), not a run timestamp, so re-runs are idempotent. Genuinely new domain for the catalog: nothing else covers births, fertility or family formation (au-population is ERP/migration; au-mortality is deaths). sites.name: aurora-australis
sites.description: A live Aurora Australis (Southern Lights) forecast for Australia — NOAA's five raw space-weather feeds fused into one plain-language answer to the only question an aurora chaser has: can I see it from my part of Australia tonight, and why? Realtime and ENTIRELY client-side (no server, no scheduled Actions, the NEMWatch/DSN-Watch class): the browser fetches the public, keyless, CORS-enabled NOAA SWPC endpoints directly and re-polls each proportional to how fast it changes — solar wind every minute, the OVATION aurora oval every ~5 min, Kp every 10 min — with a visible 'updated Xs ago' stamp. The interpretation layer is the point: it turns a raw planetary Kp number into a per-place chance using each of ~16 curated southern viewing locations' community-standard minimum Kp and approximate corrected geomagnetic latitude (Cockle Creek/Hobart need Kp ~3.5-4, Melbourne/Adelaide ~6, Sydney/Perth ~7.5, Brisbane ~8.5) — the reason Tasmania sees aurora so much more easily than its map latitude suggests (the south magnetic pole sits south of Australia). Five tab-views: Tonight (a severity-coloured verdict headline from the 3-day peak Kp, a hand-rolled semicircular Kp gauge 0-9 on the NOAA G-storm ramp, live Bz/speed/density/Bt driver tiles with good-bad cues, and the signature ranked 'Where can you see it?' city leaderboard with chance bars, click-to-drill drawer showing needed-Kp, geomag latitude, local darkness and the next likely night window); Sky Map (a Leaflet dark-basemap map of southern Australia + the Southern Ocean with the live OVATION oval rendered to a canvas image-overlay heatmap and city markers coloured by chance, real ABS state boundaries, hover tooltips, click-to-drawer); Forecast (the 3-day Kp as observed+predicted bars with a storm-line, a day x 3-hour-slot heatmap that rings the Australian-darkness windows since aurora is only visible after dark, plus NOAA's human forecast-discussion text); Solar Wind (hand-rolled SVG Bz/speed/density/Bt line charts over the last 6 h with a southward-Bz explainer); and Alerts (the live NOAA watches/warnings/alerts feed, aurora-relevant first, + a 7-day Kp history). Deliberately dark-themed — the audience uses it at night in the field to preserve night vision, and the subject IS the night sky. Dependency-free unit-tested model (its own SWPC parsers robust to BOTH shapes NOAA ships — array-of-objects and header+array-of-arrays — plus the Kp/G-scale/verdict/city-chance/oval logic in src/model.ts, and positional SVG-layout maths in src/layout.ts, shared with 61 vitest tests): parser tests on both feed shapes incl. malformed-row rejection, positional layout tests (bar/grid/line: in-bounds, no overlap, flush, value-proportional, no NaN), and a headless jsdom render of all four non-map views + the city drawer for every location against realistic live state asserting no NaN/undefined/Infinity plus a no-data degradation case. Verified additionally by a live end-to-end check that fetched TODAY's real NOAA feeds through the exact model (60 Kp-observed + 81 forecast points, 65,160-point oval reaching -50 deg lat, current Kp 1.67 Quiet / peak 4.33 -> 'camera aurora from Tasmania', Bz 0.59 nT, speed 397 km/s, 125 alerts, correct Cockle-Creek-Good/mainland-Camera gradient — all assertions pass). Genuinely new domain for the catalog: nothing else covers space weather, aurora, or the Sun-Earth connection. NOAA SWPC data is U.S. Government public domain; attribution preserved in the About panel + footer.

sites.name: au-waste
sites.description: Twelve years of Australia's National Waste Report (2006-07 to 2020-21) turned into one explorer built around the idea a single recycling number hides: whether waste is recovered depends almost entirely on what it's made of. Headline (2020-21): Australia generated 75.8 Mt of waste (up from 63 Mt, ~3 t/person) and kept 63.1% out of landfill — up from 49.7% in 2006-07 against an 80%-by-2030 National Waste Policy target — but metals are recovered at 87.1% and building rubble at 80% while PLASTICS are recovered at just 13.4% (2.28 Mt of 2.63 Mt landfilled), the lowest of any material, with textiles 21% and unclassified 19% close behind. The signature Where-it-goes view is a hand-rolled bipartite Sankey from 11 material categories to their fate (recycling / energy recovery / reuse / disposal-to-landfill / long-term storage), band width = tonnes, with a jurisdiction+year selector and click-to-highlight-and-drill; the second story is the household-bin surprise (MSW recovers ~51% vs construction's 78%, and the household stream is the SMALLEST of the three at ~14 Mt behind C&I 33 Mt and C&D 29 Mt). sites.name: au-sharks
sites.description: Every recorded shark–human incident in Australia from 1791 to 2022 — all 1,196 records from the Australian Shark-Incident Database (Taronga Conservation Society Australia with Flinders University and NSW DPI; Riley et al. 2022, Scientific Data 9:378) — turned into one explorer built around the idea a single 'shark attack' headline hides: they are rare, and most people survive. Headline: about 79% of incidents with a known outcome are survived (250 fatal of 1,196), a third (33%) are PROVOKED (person was fishing, spearfishing, feeding or handling a shark), and the signature finding — the fatality rate has fallen from ~35% before 1940 to ~10% since 2000 even as recorded incidents rose to record highs (the 2000s and 2010s are the two busiest decades on record), because faster rescue and modern trauma medicine turn once-fatal bites survivable, not because sharks changed. Three species (white 361, tiger 229, bull 197) cause nearly every death; the wobbegong has 200 incidents and zero fatalities (defensive nips). Swimming is both the most common activity (451) and the deadliest (~35% fatal) while board-riders are bitten almost as often (281) but die far less (~10%). Strong southern-summer peak (Jan busiest), 90% male victims, median age 25. Eight views: Overview (the 1-in-10-vs-1-in-3 hero, outcome donut, species/activity/state bars, decade stacks); a real Leaflet map (every geolocated incident as an outcome-coloured dot hugging the coast, plus state choropleths for total / per-million residents / fatal share, per-incident and per-state drawers painting above Leaflet); Over time (decade stacked columns by outcome + the falling fatality-rate line + per-year totals); Species (a squarified treemap by incidents, fatal-count and fatal-rate bars, and a species × activity cross-reference heatmap); Activities (leaderboard table with outcome split, fatal-rate and provoked-share bars); Seasons (month stacked columns by outcome + time-of-day bars debunking the dawn/dusk myth); a searchable/sortable Explorer of all 1,196 records with a click-to-filter decade histogram; and auto-detected Insights — plus hash-linkable incident (#i=1187), state (#s=NSW) and species (#sp=white) drill-down drawers, a glossary and an honest About panel. Dependency-free unit-tested pipeline (its own tab-delimited reader + canonicalisers in pipeline/parse.mjs, shared with 49 tests) with TWO reconciliation gates on INDEPENDENTLY-recorded fields so agreement proves a correct parse: (1) ≥98% of geolocated incidents must fall inside Australia's bounding box (99.7% actual — a lat/lng swap or column shift pushes coordinates outside, and the tests deliberately swap them to prove the gate fails), and (2) the recorded State column must agree with a coarse coordinate→state classifier for ≥90% of records (99.2% actual — the tests rotate the state column to prove this fails). Traps handled: the source codes board-riding (surfing) as 'boarding' and standing-in-water as an 'other:' activity (canonicalised); stray numeric values in the gender column from a couple of shifted source rows are coerced to unknown rather than crashing; missing species/age/length shown as '—' never guessed; framed carefully throughout as a rare event and a conservation/safety tool, not sensationalism. State boundaries vendored in-repo (pipeline/au-states.geojson, ABS ASGS 2021) so CI reconciles without the factory patterns dir. Annual data pipeline (ASID publishes a refreshed public version roughly yearly) — the slowest proportional cadence; embeds the data year range (1791-2022), not a run timestamp, so re-runs are idempotent. Genuinely new domain for the catalog — nothing else covers wildlife or marine safety. ASID data is MIT-licensed; attribution to Taronga/Flinders/NSW DPI + the Scientific Data paper preserved in the About panel and footer.

sites.description: Fifty years of short-term overseas arrivals to Australia — the ABS Overseas Arrivals and Departures release (OAD_COUNTRY + OAD_REASON, monthly 1975-07 to 2026-05, 611 months) turned into one explorer built around the single most dramatic data event in modern Australian statistics: when the border closed, short-term visitor arrivals fell from a pre-pandemic peak of 1,077,720 in December 2019 to just 2,250 in April 2020 — a 99.8% collapse, the sharpest fall in the entire record by a wide margin. Two traveller flows: short-term VISITORS ARRIVING (people who live overseas, by country of residence — inbound tourism) and short-term RESIDENTS RETURNING (Australians home from a short trip, by country visited). Headline: the last 12 months brought 9.16m visitors, ~97% of the same months in 2019 (recovery 96.8%), but the recovery is wildly uneven by country — Nepal 166% and India well past 2019, while China sits at 78% and Malaysia at 57%. New Zealand is the single largest source (1.44m, 15.8% of arrivals), then China (1.13m, 12.3%). Nine views: Overview (the 2,250 cliff hero, recovery gauge, top-source and region bars, both-directions line); the signature Recovery view (the full 50-year monthly line with the Feb-2020-to-Feb-2022 border-closure band, a monthly/12-month-average smoothing toggle, an is-tourism-back gauge, and a recovery-by-region bar with a 2019 tick); a real Leaflet + Natural Earth world choropleth of arrivals by source country (visitors/returns log ramp + a recovery-vs-2019 diverging mode), per-country drawer painting above Leaflet; Compare countries (the killer rebased multi-line — each country indexed to its own 2019 monthly average so a small market like Nepal and a huge one like China share one axis, with a dashed 2019 reference line, plus recovered-most / furthest-below movers lists); Why (reason-for-journey — holiday/VFR/business/education/employment/conference — as a 100%-stacked area over time + a now-vs-2019 dumbbell, holiday 45% of visitor reasons); Length of stay (intended-duration distribution now vs 2019 + a stay-mix stacked area); Seasonality (a year x month calendar heatmap on an absolute-log or within-year scale that makes the December-January peak, the long-run growth, and the 2020-21 COVID hole all visible at once); a searchable/sortable Explorer of all 57 countries with visitor sparklines and a click-to-filter recovery-distribution histogram; and auto-detected Insights — plus a hash-linkable per-country drawer (#c=6101) with a 50-year visitors-and-returns line, recovery, ranks, and key figures. Distinct from au-visas (temporary visa STOCK — who is here on what visa) and au-population (permanent net overseas migration): this is short-term MOVEMENT, border crossings not people. Dependency-free unit-tested pipeline (its own RFC-4180/SDMX-CSV reader + continent-hierarchy builder in pipeline/lib/parse.mjs, shared with 48 tests) with TWO reconciliation gates on INDEPENDENTLY-published columns: (1) an EXACT cross-flow total gate — total short-term arrivals in OAD_COUNTRY must equal the total in OAD_REASON every month (0 mismatches / 611 for visitors, 0 / 227 for returns), and (2) a rounding-TOLERANT continental gate — each region's member countries + its Other residual must sum to the published TOn subtotal, enforced from 2004 where the country breakdown is complete (ABS randomly rounds every count to the nearest 10 for privacy, so exact sums are impossible; a real parse error still fails everywhere including modern months). Data traps handled: blank OBS_VALUE = not published, coerced to null not 0; the SACC not-stated codes (NI, 0000) trail the last continent in the codelist and were leaking into Sub-Saharan Africa's member sum until the hierarchy builder was fixed to admit only country codes and OTn residuals (a bug the tolerant gate caught); the ABS only broke out the full ~57 individual countries from ~2003, so deep history is sparser for small markets while national totals stay complete; seasonally-adjusted series are absent from OAD_COUNTRY so the smooth recovery line is a client-side 12-month rolling mean of the original series; 57 SACC numeric country codes hand-mapped to ISO3 for the Natural Earth join (all 57 shaded; the rest of each region sits in an Other group with no single polygon). Monthly data pipeline (ABS publishes OAD about five weeks after each reference month) — the fastest cadence the factory allows and it matches the source; embeds the latest data month (2026-05), not a run timestamp, so re-runs are idempotent.

sites.name: au-inflation
sites.description: Australia's Consumer Price Index turned from the ABS's dry index tables into one interface built around the one idea a single inflation figure hides: not everything gets more expensive. The whole 158-item CPI basket (11 groups → subgroups → 87 expenditure classes), 8 capital cities plus the weighted average, quarterly 1948→2025-Q3, joined to the Wage Price Index. Headline: overall inflation was 3.2% over the year to September 2025 — but since 2000 tobacco is up 837% (excise-driven), medical services +301%, gas +300%, secondary education +288%, electricity +228%, while audio/visual/computing equipment fell 90%, women's garments −22%, telecoms −18% and 14 basket items are cheaper now than in 2000. The signature Risers & Fallers view is a diverging ranked bar of every item's cumulative price change since a selectable base year (amber→red up, green down) — the story a headline number can't show, because it IS the spread between winners and losers. The second story is the cost-of-living crunch: wages (WPI) rose 141% since 1997 vs prices 116% (real +12%), but since 2020 wages rose 19.3% while prices rose 23.6% — a −3.5% real pay cut, the sharpest real-wage decline in the series. sites.name: au-baby-names
sites.description: Every name in the top-100 boys' and girls' lists that New South Wales (from 1952) and Queensland (from 1960) have published each year — 824 distinct names across 28,034 yearly rankings, with real baby counts — turned into an explorer built around the one idea a single year's top-10 list hides: naming has fragmented. The signature finding is that the #1 name isn't what it used to be: NSW's most popular boys' name went from John (2,205 babies, 39.5% of the top 100 shared the top-10 names) in 1952 to Noah (589 babies, 22.8% top-10 share) in 2025 — fewer babies given the leading name even as the population grew, and the top-10 concentration nearly halved. Deliberately NOT geographic (name×year×sex is temporal ranking data, so no map — the signature form is a bump chart, exactly right for how a ranking evolves). Ten views: Overview (John→Noah hero, this year's #1 boy/girl per state, the two concentration stats, top-10 lists); Name Finder (the killer searchable feature — type any name, chart its rank/count trajectory across 74 years, compare several, deep-linkable, e.g. John declining from #1 while Noah/Charlotte rocket up from outside the top 100 since ~1998); The Charts (a hand-rolled SVG bump chart of the top names over time with hover-highlight + zoom/pan); Diversity (the signature analytical view — four falling top-10-concentration lines + the #1-name count over time, both making the fragmentation argument); Risers & Fallers (biggest climbers/fallers over 1/10/25/all-year windows + flash-in-the-pan names that peaked once and vanished); Unisex (names in both sexes' lists, gender balance); First Letters (a warm heatmap of first-initial share by decade — J-names of the 1950s giving way to A/E names today); NSW vs QLD (state face-off with the more-popular-in-one-state skew); a searchable/sortable Explorer with a first-appearance histogram that click-filters; and auto-detected Insights — plus a hash-linkable per-name drawer (#name=Noah) with rank/count trajectory and where the babies are by state and sex. Dependency-free unit-tested pipeline (its own RFC-4180 reader + normalisers in pipeline/parse.mjs, shared with 47 tests) that normalises three different source shapes — NSW's long CSV (Rank/Name/Number/Gender/Year), QLD's per-year WIDE files (Girl Names/Count/Boy Names/Count, row order = rank), and QLD's 1960-2005 long file (no rank) — into one record stream, with a HARD reconciliation gate: for every source that publishes an ordering (NSW's Rank column, QLD's per-year row order), the parsed count must be non-increasing along that order within each (state,year,sex) group, 0 violations across 188 ordered groups, or the build fails — a swapped Name/Number column breaks monotonicity, so agreement proves a correct parse. Coverage is framed honestly throughout: NSW + QLD are the two states that publish long, open, count-level histories (VIC/WA/SA/etc. publish only short/rank-only lists → logged as expansion ideas), together ~45% of Australian births; only the top 100 per year is released, so a name leaving a chart means it left the top 100, not that it vanished; spellings counted separately; registration year not birth year. Annual data pipeline (both registries publish the prior year each January-March) — the slowest proportional cadence; embeds the latest data year, not a run timestamp.

sites.name: au-safeguard
sites.description: Australia's biggest industrial carbon emitters, turned from the Clean Energy Regulator's two bare annual CSVs into an explorer built around the one question a headline emissions total can't answer: which specific facilities came in OVER their government-set baseline, and by how much. The Safeguard Mechanism covers every facility emitting >100,000 tCO2-e/yr; each has a legally-declining baseline (net zero by 2050). Headline (2024-25): 148 of 228 covered facilities emitted above their own cap — 133.8 Mt covered against a 128.1 Mt aggregate baseline, ~a quarter of Australia's whole footprint. Two things the raw number hides carry the site: 17% of it is fugitive METHANE (61% of coal mining's emissions — the gas venting from the seam, not the diesel in the machines), and the scheme leans on OFFSETS — 13.1M carbon credits surrendered to cover excess vs just 6.7M SMCs earned by facilities that beat baseline. The signature Over-the-Line view is a log-log scatter of baseline (x) vs emitted (y) with the y=x at-baseline diagonal, so 'big' and 'over' visibly split apart (Gorgon is #1 by size but only #6 by excess; small coal mines sit far above the line). Nine views: Overview (148-of-228 hero, over/under split, gas bar, top-10 + sector previews); Over the Line (the scatter with zoom/pan + furthest-over/under diverging bars); a real Leaflet state choropleth (covered/over-baseline/count/methane, diverging ramp for net position, per-state facility panel + facility drawer painting above Leaflet); Sectors (squarified treemap by ANZSIC, coal+gas dominate, click to drill); Companies (facilities rolled up to parent responsible emitter via a curated BHP/Glencore/Rio/Chevron/Woodside/Santos map); Carbon Market (SMCs earned vs ACCUs/SMCs surrendered, per-sector + leaderboards); Gases (100%-stacked gas mix by industry — coal mining literally 61% methane — + methane-intensity leaderboard); a searchable/sortable Explorer with a covered/baseline-ratio distribution histogram (mass just above 100%) that click-filters the table; and auto-detected Insights — plus a hash-linkable per-facility drawer (#f=gorgon-operations) with baseline-vs-emitted bars, gas donut, rank, credits and net position. Dependency-free unit-tested pipeline (its own RFC-4180 reader + sentinel/company/sector canonicalisers in pipeline/parse.mjs, shared with 51 tests incl. a headless jsdom render of every view against the real built data) with TWO hard reconciliation gates, both on INDEPENDENTLY-published columns so agreement proves a correct parse: for every facility CO2+CH4+N2O+Other == covered emissions (0 mismatches/228), and for every settled facility net position == net emissions - baseline (0 mismatches/96). sites.name: au-population
sites.description: Where Australia is growing and shrinking — the ABS Regional Population release (Estimated Resident Population by LGA 2001-2024, plus the components of population change) for all 547 local government areas, joined to real ABS ASGS 2024 LGA boundaries, built around the one idea a single growth number hides: growth has three engines that point in completely different directions across the country — natural increase (births minus deaths), net internal migration (movement within Australia, zero-sum nationally) and net overseas migration. Headline: Australia reached 27,194,369 people in 2024, and net overseas migration added 435,198 of the year's growth against just 106,394 from natural increase — migration, not babies, is now ~4x the larger engine, and it is also the most volatile: net overseas migration collapsed to -87,876 in 2021 (the first net loss on record, when the border closed) then rebounded to a record +535,518 in 2023. The signature Growth Engines view is a quadrant scatter of natural-increase rate (x) against net-migration rate (y) that sorts every council into four demographic types a league table cannot: 'growing on both engines' (272 councils, e.g. outer-Melbourne Melton +6.6% on internal migration 37.8/1,000), 'migration-fed, natural decline' (154 councils — ageing sea-change coasts that grow only because people move in while deaths outnumber births), 'natural growth, net outflow' (101), and 'emptying' (20 councils declining on both, e.g. the Wimmera wheat-belt shires Hindmarsh and Buloke). The against-the-grain contrasts the decomposition surfaces: inner-city Melbourne grew 6.5% on overseas arrivals (78/1,000) while LOSING residents internally (-19.6/1,000), the opposite of the outer corridors; and net internal migration is zero-sum, so NSW's loss (-31k) is Queensland's gain (+50k) — the Sydney->Brisbane drift. Nine views: an Overview (hero, the three national engine bars, fastest-growing/shrinking/most-added/most-overseas-fed tiles, top movers, the four-type split bar, 23-year national trend); the signature Growth Engines quadrant scatter (zoom/pan, state filter, click->council) + biggest-movers decomposition bars; a real Leaflet choropleth of all 547 LGAs across five measures (growth 1yr/5yr, natural/internal/overseas rate, population) with a per-council drawer painting above Leaflet; Rankings across seven metrics vs the national median; Trends (the three engines over time with the COVID border-closure band, plus 24-year population by state); a nested state->LGA population Treemap coloured by growth; a States matrix (state x engine per-capita heatmap + engine-composition bars); a searchable/sortable Explorer of every council with population sparklines, signed engine mini-bars and a click-through growth-rate histogram; and auto-detected Insights — plus a hash-linkable per-council drill-down (#lga=10050) with a 2001-2024 population sparkline, the engine breakdown, births/deaths, and rank vs national. Dependency-free, unit-tested pipeline (its own RFC-4180 SDMX-CSV reader in pipeline/parse.mjs, shared with 46 tests incl. a headless jsdom render smoke test that renders every view + every drawer against the real built data asserting no NaN) with a HARD reconciliation gate: two INDEPENDENTLY-published ABS series must agree — the long annual ERP series and the component-file's own ERP (POP_COMP=10) match for every one of the 547 LGAs (0 mismatches), and net internal migration must sum to ~0 nationally (it sums to exactly 0) — or the build fails. Data handled: components stitched across ERP_COMP_LGA2021 (2017-2021) + ERP_COMP_LGA2024 (2022-2024) keeping only codes in the 2024 boundary set so edition drift can't invent regions; the national components trend summed from the kept LGAs because the AUS row only exists for 2022-2024, cross-checked against the published AUS total; blank OBS_VALUE coerced to null not 0; intercensal rebasing means components don't sum exactly to ERP change, framed honestly. Annual data pipeline (ABS publishes Regional Population each March/April) — the slowest proportional cadence; embeds the ABS reference year, not a run timestamp, so re-runs are idempotent.

sites.name: au-vehicles
sites.description: Every road vehicle registered in Australia — 22,305,347 at the 31 January 2025 BITRE snapshot, of which 16,080,036 are passenger cars — by fuel type, year of manufacture, make/model, vehicle type and postcode, from BITRE's Road Vehicles Australia (the successor to the discontinued ABS Motor Vehicle Census, derived from state registries via NEVDIS). Built around the one idea a single fuel-mix number hides — stock vs flow: battery-electric cars are just 1.55% of the cars ON THE ROAD, but 8.6% of cars BUILT in 2024 and 35.5% of them are electrified (hybrid+electric), because the fleet is a slow-moving stock (median build year 2015, ~10 years old) not this year's sales. The signature New-Car Effect view teaches this with a year-of-manufacture slider that morphs the fuel donut/bar from the whole fleet (5.9% electrified) to the newest cohort (35.5%) — the au-unis 4/6/9-year / au-approvals approvals-vs-completions pattern. The against-the-grain second story: the biggest fuel shift of the last decade isn't petrol->electric, it's petrol->diesel — there is 9.4x more diesel (14.6%) than battery-electric (1.55%) in the car fleet, diesel has risen every year 2021->2025, and the light-commercial ute/van fleet is 77% diesel while trucks are 97-99% and motorcycles 99% petrol. Nine views: an Overview (hero 9.4x ratio, fuel donut, stat tiles, fuel-by-type preview); the New-Car Effect (slider + 100%-stacked fuel-mix-by-model-year area annotated with the 2019 first-EVs and 2022 BYD/MG arrival + fleet-age histogram + median-age/EV-share by state); a real Leaflet POA choropleth of all 2,640 postcodes across electric %, electrified %, diesel %, petrol % and total (skew-tuned green ramp set from the actual quantiles, per-postcode drawer painting above Leaflet); Rankings (postcode + state leaderboards by each fuel); Trends (5 annual snapshots, national 100%-area + per-state multi-line with an Electric/Electrified/Diesel toggle + then-vs-now change table); Makes & Models (zoomable squarified make treemap coloured by dominant fuel — Toyota 3.25M, then top models and every EV model: Tesla Model 3 63k, Model Y 59k, BYD Atto 3, MG4); Vehicle Types (fuel-mix bars per type + a type x fuel row-share heatmap); a searchable/sortable Explorer of every postcode with a fuel mini-bar and an electric-share distribution histogram that click-filters the table; and auto-detected Insights — plus a hash-linkable per-postcode drill-down (#postcode=3000) with fuel donut, rank vs national, and every fuel type. Dependency-free unit-tested pipeline (its own RFC-4180 reader + canonicalisers in pipeline/parse.mjs, shared with 37 tests) resolving every BITRE resource URL via the data.gov.au CKAN API by filename pattern so re-hosted files still resolve next year. Data traps handled: the 'Total' pseudo-state row (excluded — zeroed in the detailed extract but would rank as a state); year-of-manufacture '-'/'Not stated' sentinels; six motive-power labels canonicalised to five fuel classes (Dual fuel/Other/'-' -> Other); privacy PERTURBATION + <3 suppression means interior sums never equal published totals, so the HARD reconciliation gate is tolerant — the independently-aggregated state-file and postcode-file national passenger totals must agree within 1.5% (matched to 0.02%) and the national total must sit in range, or the build fails; boundary POA_CODE21 renamed to `pc` so the choropleth joins (a bug caught in verification where every polygon painted 'no data' grey). Annual data pipeline (BITRE publishes a January registry snapshot once a year, released mid-year) — the slowest proportional cadence; embeds the BITRE snapshot date, not a run timestamp. Framing throughout: this is the STOCK of registered vehicles (not sales), EV = battery/fuel-cell electric, 'electrified' = hybrid+electric, and keeping a car ~11 years is why the fleet lags the showroom.

sites.name: au-foreign-owned
sites.description: The ATO's Register of Foreign Ownership of Australian Assets — all six asset classes (agricultural land, water entitlements, residential & commercial land, business interests, mining & exploration tenements) — unified into one interface built around the finding that there is no single biggest foreign owner of Australia: it flips completely by asset. At 30 June 2025, five different countries lead the six classes — the United Kingdom tops farmland (7.66M ha, having just overtaken China), the United States commercial property ($21.8bn of $67.1bn) and mining tenements, China residential purchases (1,134 buyers), Canada water entitlements (1,066 GL), and the Cayman Islands (a fund domicile) business interests (771). ~13% of Australian farmland and 12.7% of water carry a foreign interest, both broadly flat for a decade. The signature story runs against the political grain: China has SOLD DOWN ~29% of its farmland from a ~9.2M ha peak in 2019-20 to 6.54M ha, not bought up; Canada roughly doubled 2023->2024. Eight views: an Overview with six 'flip cards' (one #1 country per class); the signature Atlas country x asset-class rank matrix (the inversion at a glance); a country leaderboard with 9-year farmland sparklines; a Leaflet state choropleth of foreign-ownership % (farmland/water) or count (other classes) with per-state drawer; Trends (the UK/China farmland crossover multi-line, foreign-share-% over time, residential acquisition flow); By asset (squarified country-composition treemap + industry/land-use/property-type breakdowns); a searchable/sortable Explorer of every country across all six classes; and auto-detected Insights — plus hash-linkable per-country (#c=Canada) and per-state (#s=NT) drill-downs. Dependency-free, unit-tested Node pipeline (its own zip+xlsx reader in pipeline/parse.mjs, shared with the tests) with a HARD reconciliation gate: the ag 'Level of foreign ownership' total and the independently-published 'Foreign/Australian share' total must agree exactly at the latest year (both 50,262,369 ha) or the build fails. Traps handled: Excel-serial dates (45838=30-Jun-2025); deliberately-MISLABELLED units (column headers say "'000 hectares"/"gigalitres"/"$ million" but the values are raw hectares/megalitres/dollars, and Table 1 / the water country table switch units mid-column — normalised by magnitude and cross-checked against the reliable published % column); '<=5' small-cell suppression coerced to null not zero; country-name variants and typos ('United kingdom', 'Belguim', 'Hong Kong, SAR' vs '(SAR)') canonicalised to one entity with ISO codes so joins work across the six workbooks; NSW/ACT combined in ag/water/mining (ACT inherits the value on the map); source country = country of CONTROL not incorporation (why Cayman/BVI/Bermuda loom large), framed carefully throughout. Annual pipeline (the ATO reports once a year) that embeds the ATO report date, not a run timestamp.

sites.name: au-election
sites.description: Australia's 2025 federal election (House of Representatives, all 150 seats) unified from the AEC's ~40 separate CSV exports (Tally Room event 31496) into one interface built around the two things a raw seat count hides: the swing and preferences. Headline: the Albanese Labor government returned decisively with 94 seats and 55.22% two-party-preferred (+3.09 swing), Coalition 43, Greens 1, ten independents, KAP + Centre Alliance 2. Nine views: an Overview (parliament horseshoe with the crossbench between the majors, TPP bar, record-low 66.4% major-party primary), a Leaflet choropleth of all 150 real electoral-division polygons in winner/TPP/swing modes with a per-seat drawer, the signature Mackerras pendulum (every seat ranked by margin, coloured by who ACTUALLY holds it so teal seats show as teal pips on the Coalition-notional side) with a live uniform-swing simulator that tallies notional seats and lists which seats flip, a preference-flow Sankey (Greens 88% -> Labor, One Nation 75% -> Coalition, all minors 60.7% -> Labor), first preferences with a party x state matrix, rankings across six metrics, a searchable/sortable explorer of all 150 seats, margin + swing distribution histograms with click-through, and auto-detected insights (Dutton lost Dickson; Bradfield decided by 26 votes; 20 seats changed hands) — plus a hash-linkable per-seat drill-down (#v=map&seat=Dickson) with every candidate's first preferences, the two-candidate pair, notional TPP, turnout and informal. Dependency-free unit-tested pipeline (its own RFC-4180 reader in pipeline/parse.mjs, shared with tests) that reconciles three independently-published AEC totals (150 seats by group == 150 by member == first-pref Elected column; national TPP ALP ~55.2%) and fails the build on drift. The signature data trap handled: three seats non-classic in 2022 (Brisbane, Bendigo, Nicholls) have no comparable prior two-party figure, so the AEC's raw Swing column equals the current ALP TPP percentage as a sentinel — taken at face value these become absurd +59/+51/-36 'swings' that skew the national average, the swing rankings and the map; detected (|swing - ALP%| < 0.05) and nulled, excluded from swing rankings/insights/histogram, drawn grey on the map, and the national swing taken as the correct aggregate (55.22 - the 52.13 2022 national result = +3.09) rather than the mean of divisional swings. Reuses the fleet's Digital Atlas electoral-division boundaries (150 real polygons). Yearly pipeline (a federal election is ~3-yearly and final results never change) that embeds the AEC Generated timestamp, not a run time, so re-runs are idempotent.

sites.name: au-imprisonment
sites.description: The ABS Prisoners in Australia 2025 release turned into one interface built around the two things a single imprisonment rate hides: who is inside, and whether they have been sentenced. Headline: 46,998 adults in prison on 30 June 2025 (rate 216.4 per 100,000, up 21% since 2016). The signature finding — and the reason the whole site exists — is over-representation: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are imprisoned about 16.8x as often as non-Indigenous people age-standardised (2,500 vs 149 per 100,000), and the gap has WIDENED from 10.6x in 2016, not narrowed; age-standardising barely changes it, so it is not explained by the two populations having different age structures. The worst over-representation ratio is the ACT (23x) and WA (20x) — not the NT that people assume (18.5x), because the NT's overall rate is highest but its non-Indigenous base rate is also high. Almost all growth since 2016 is one group: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander numbers +64% while non-Indigenous stayed roughly flat. The second story is remand: 42.2% of prisoners are unsentenced (presumed innocent), up from 31.2% in 2016, and this group drove most of the growth; the most remand-heavy major offence is Acts intended to cause injury (assault) at 59% unsentenced. Nine views: Overview (hero + the two gradients + sentenced/remand stacked area); The Gap (signature ranked dumbbell of each state's Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islander vs non-Indigenous rate on a log axis, crude/age-standardised toggle showing the gap survives standardisation, plus the widening national ratio line); a Leaflet choropleth of 8 states across 4 measures shaded relative to the national figure; Remand (share-over-time line, time-on-remand histogram, per-state remand share); Offences (squarified treemap of the 16 ANZSOC divisions coloured by remand share, offence x legal-status split, change since 2016); Who's inside (age x sex population pyramid + age-imprisonment-rate curve + composition); Prisons (state-coloured treemap of 112 facilities with zoom + searchable list; biggest is Casuarina WA at 1,680); Rankings (states vs national on any metric + full table with rate sparklines); and auto-detected Insights — plus a hash-linkable per-state drawer (#v=map&s=WA). Dependency-free, unit-tested xlsx pipeline (its own zip+xlsx reader in pipeline/parse.mjs, shared with the tests) whose HARD reconciliation gate asserts the two INDEPENDENTLY-published national totals agree exactly (Table 5 offence total == Table 2 characteristics total == 46,998) and fails the build on drift; component cell sums are ABS-perturbed (the T4/T9/T34 footnotes) so state/offence/remand/facility sums are checked with tolerance + warnings, never a hard fail. Parse traps handled: a data-row year must be EXACTLY a 4-digit label (rowYear) or the last state block over-runs into footnotes and the trailing 'Australia' national block (ACT absorbed both, doubling the total); footnote markers stripped from labels; np/../-/n.a. string sentinels coerced to null not 0; state header labels (Vic./Qld/Tas./Aust.) mapped to codes; FP noise rounded. Careful framing throughout: measures imprisonment (a justice-system outcome) not offending, remand = unsentenced/presumed innocent, most serious offence/charge only, ABS terminology 'Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander', no place or group framed as a scoreboard, Lifeline/13YARN in the footer and About panel. Annual data pipeline (ABS publishes Prisoners in Australia each December) — the slowest proportional cadence; embeds the ABS release date, not a run timestamp, so re-runs are idempotent.

sites.name: au-branches
sites.description: Every physical banking point in Australia — bank branch, Bank@Post, other face-to-face counter and bank-owned ATM — from APRA's annual ADI Points of Presence return, nine June snapshots 2017-2025 (137,000 raw rows), joined to ABS resident population and real ASGS 2021 SA3 boundaries. The one idea that makes the data readable: as branches collapsed, Australia Post's Bank@Post barely moved, so in hundreds of towns the post office counter has quietly become the last place to bank. Headline: branches fell 5,694 -> 3,205 (-44%) in eight years and bank-owned ATMs -63% (13,814 -> 5,143), but Bank@Post held at -6% (3,578 -> 3,365). At the town (SA2) grain, 366 towns lost their LAST branch since 2017 — home to ~4.4m residents — of which 298 keep a Bank@Post and 68 have no staffed banking of any kind. EFTPOS (the ~700k shop card terminals) is deliberately excluded as merchant payment, not banking access. Nine views: an Overview hero + 'great substitution' stacked-area (branch draining while Bank@Post holds) + remoteness loss bars; a real Leaflet POINT map of all ~10,460 service points in 2025 (canvas renderer, channel layer toggles, colour by channel) that switches to an SA3 per-capita access choropleth (branches per 10,000 residents, ratio-cut ramp); the signature Banking Deserts view (SA2 towns that lost their last branch, filterable by state/remoteness/safety-net, with a people-affected total and a Bank@Post-vs-nothing split bar); Who's Closing (per-institution closure leaderboard with rank-by toggle, a bank x year retreat matrix shaded against each bank's own peak, and a squarified institution treemap coloured by sector); Remoteness equity (branches per 100k by remoteness over time as a multi-line, a Bank@Post-reliance bar, and a remoteness x channel per-100k matrix); Rankings across four metrics with a click-to-filter distribution histogram; an annotated national + per-state Timeline; a searchable/sortable Explorer of all 340 SA3s with branch sparklines; and auto-detected Insights — plus hash-linkable per-region (#r=sa3) and per-institution (#b=abn) drill-down drawers. Data traps handled in a dependency-free, unit-tested pipeline (its own minimal zip+xlsx reader in pipeline/parse.mjs, shared with the tests): (1) Table 2's embedded 'Population by SA2' is actually at SUBURB grain so it repeats per suburb and only covers SA2s that HAVE a service — summing double-counts and it undercounts regional population, so per-capita denominators use full ABS ERP by SA3 (all 340 regions incl. zero-branch ones) not Table 2; SA2 population for the deserts 'people affected' figure dedupes Table 2 to one value per SA2; (2) EFTPOS excluded; (3) APRA SA3 names occasionally arrive truncated (a shared-string cut, e.g. 'Augusta - Margaret River - Busselto[n]') so the name->code join has a unique-prefix fallback (324/325 exact, 100% after fallback); (4) the pipeline asserts region branch totals reconcile to >=97% of the national branch total and fails the build on drift (matched 100%). Annual data pipeline (APRA publishes each October) — the slowest proportional cadence.

sites.name: au-mortality
sites.description: The AIHW's Mortality Over Regions and Time (MORT) release — published as ~60 separate Excel workbooks — turned into one interface covering all eight geography levels (342 SA3s, 549 LGAs, 91 SA4s, 33 PHNs, states, capital-city splits, remoteness areas, socioeconomic quintiles) across 2020-2024, plus the top-20 leading causes of death per region pooled over the five years (128 distinct causes). Headline: Australia registered 187,268 deaths in 2024, of which 29,123 were POTENTIALLY AVOIDABLE — 49% of every death before age 75. The site is built around the one idea that makes this data readable and that a raw rate actively hides: a crude death rate mostly measures how OLD a place is, not how healthy it is. The signature Age Illusion view therefore ranks every SA3 twice — crude and age-standardised — and joins them with a line so the reader watches regions swap ends of the table: Kimberley ranks 238th of 322 on the raw rate and 3rd once standardised, while Bribie - Beachmere goes from 15th to 238th (a retirement coast, not an unhealthy one); 180 of 322 regions move at least 50 places. A slope chart rather than a scatter because a scatter shows only that the two measures correlate, while the crossing IS the argument; labels are de-collided with leader lines on both axes. Two structural gradients carry the rest and both ship pre-computed in the source, so nothing is estimated: avoidable death is 2.8x higher in Very Remote Australia (244.5 vs 86.4 per 100,000) with a 13.3-year gap in median age at death, and the most disadvantaged fifth of areas lose 2.4x as many lives to avoidable causes as the least (143.8 vs 61.0). Katherine tops the country at 342.1 against Ku-ring-gai's 36.7 — 9.3x. Nine views: overview with both gradients and a five-year national trend; the Age Illusion; a Leaflet choropleth of 340 SA3s across six measures, shaded on the RATIO to the national figure rather than quantiles (quantiles always fill every class and so manufacture difference; ratio cuts let one legend mean the same thing on every measure); rankings across five measures and five geography levels with the national median drawn on the chart plus a click-through distribution histogram; a squarified cause treemap where selecting a cause re-ranks every region by it; remoteness/socioeconomic/sex gradients as connected step charts; a cause x group matrix showing that remote Australians die of DIFFERENT things as well as sooner (diabetes 3.49x national in Very Remote, suicide 2.00x, COPD 2.04x, while dementia runs BELOW national at 0.93x); a sortable Explorer whose sparklines break at suppressed years instead of plunging to zero; and auto-computed insights — plus a hash-linkable per-region drawer (#r=SA351001). Five parse traps, each of which produces a confidently wrong number: (1) 'Top 20 leading causes' and 'All causes' are subtotal rows carrying a BLANK rank in the same column as the twenty real causes, so summing the column counts every death ~2.6x; (2) 127 geography names appear under more than one level (Tasmania is both a state and a PHN, 'Australia (total)' appears under all eight), so the join key must be the mort code and the national row must be pulled out of every level or it ranks as a region and wins; (3) blank means SUPPRESSED, not zero — 10 of 340 SA3s in 2024 including East Arnhem (pop 14,724) and Barkly, and coerced to zero the most disadvantaged regions in the country rank as the healthiest, so nulls survive to the screen as 'not published' and are excluded from rankings rather than sorted to an end; (4) the CSVs are CP1252 not UTF-8 — every ICD range uses byte 0x96 and 'Alzheimer's' uses 0x92, which latin1 turns into invisible control characters so 'I20-I25' silently renders as 'I20I25' and the pooled period as '20202024' (Node ships no cp1252 decoder and TextDecoder('windows-1252') needs full ICU, so the 32 C1 slots are mapped by hand); (5) numbers are comma-formatted strings, some quoted with embedded commas. The dependency-free pipeline asserts that Table 2's pooled 'All causes' total for Australia (894,107) reconciles exactly with the sum of Table 1's five annual death counts — the two tables are produced independently, so agreement proves the parser read both correctly — and that the twenty ranked causes sum to the published top-20 subtotal, failing the build on drift. Framing care throughout: median age at death is NOT life expectancy, deaths are counted where a person lived rather than where they died, and leading causes are each region's LOCAL top twenty so a missing cause did not rank there rather than not occurring. Suicide is the 13th leading cause nationally and far higher in remote and young cohorts, so Lifeline / Beyond Blue / 13YARN appear in the footer, the About panel and beside any suicide-specific view, and no region is ever framed as a scoreboard.

sites.name: au-threatened
sites.description: Every plant and animal on Australia's EPBC Act threatened-species list (2,208 species from the DCCEEW/SPRAT state lists, extract 2026-02-06) turned from a flat legal register into an explorable atlas — joined to real ABS ASGS 2021 state boundaries. Two findings carry the site. First, plants dominate the crisis: 1,514 of the 2,208 listed species (69%) are plants against 694 animals, more than two to one, and they skew harder to the critical end (306 CR plants) — the opposite of where public attention goes. Second, and the reason the signature Endemism view exists: 77% of listed species (1,710) occur in a single jurisdiction only, so they are endemic and would be lost from Earth if that one place changed — a fact a raw species count cannot show. Headline severity: 453 Critically Endangered, 860 Endangered, 785 Vulnerable, 102 Extinct + 1 Extinct in the Wild (mammals lead the extinctions, Australia's notorious record). Eight views: an Overview status pyramid with the plants-vs-animals split and a click-to-filter segmented bar; a Leaflet choropleth of the 8 states/territories (total / critically endangered / endemic-only, skew-aware quantile buckets) plus an off-map panel for the external territories that carry outsized endemic loads (Norfolk Is 97 species / 56 endemic, Christmas Is 36/16); a Rankings leaderboard across families/classes/genera/states with a status-metric toggle; a click-to-zoom squarified Tree-of-Life treemap (Kingdom→Class→Family, coloured by kingdom, svgZoom); the Endemism view (per-place endemic-vs-shared diverging bars + jurisdiction-span histogram); a Class×jurisdiction matrix heatmap; a searchable/filterable Explorer of all 2,208 species; and auto-detected Insights — plus hash-linkable per-species (#s=taxonId) and per-state (#state=WA) drill-down drawers. Dependency-free unit-tested pipeline (its own RFC-4180 CSV reader in pipeline/parse.mjs, shared with the test suite) that asserts the parsed status and kingdom sub-totals reconcile to the total and fails the build on drift. Parse traps handled: '-' is the empty sentinel (not a value), Common Name fields carry quoted embedded commas (multi-name), Class values like 'Streptophyta (no class)' need the suffix stripped, and endemism is computed as single-jurisdiction occurrence. Data note: occurrence is indicative (broad presence, not a range map) and a species with no jurisdiction flagged is still validly listed; the source is the legal schedule, amended a few times a year, so the pipeline crons quarterly.

sites.name: au-approvals
sites.description: Every new home Australia approves to build, mapped to the SA3 region it will go in and measured against the National Housing Accord — the ABS Building Approvals series (new residential dwelling units, monthly from Jul 2021, ~337 SA3 regions) joined to ABS resident population and real ASGS 2021 boundaries. The hero view answers the question everyone asks: over the latest 12 months Australia approved 201,349 new homes, 84% of the ~240,000/yr (20,000/mo) completions pace the 1.2-million-in-five-years Accord implies — and because approvals LEAD completions and not every approval is built, running below that line is the earliest warning the target will be missed. The Accord tracker stacks houses/townhouses/apartments monthly with that benchmark and annotates the 2022 cash-rate liftoff, the Jul-2024 Accord start and the 2025 rate cuts: rolling-12 approvals fell from a ~201k peak (Jun 2022) to a ~160k trough in 2024 and have since climbed back to the peak, still ~16% short of the pace. The second story is density, and the national average (59% detached houses) hides two different countries: outer-suburban growth corridors approve almost only houses (Melton - Bacchus Marsh tops the country at 4,638 homes/yr, 84% houses; Wanneroo 95%) while inner cities are almost pure apartment (Melbourne City 3,471 homes at 0% houses, Sydney Inner City 99% non-house), and the states split the same way — ACT 18% houses / 68% apartments against Tasmania 93% houses. Supply intensity per resident reranks everything (Molonglo in the ACT tops at 447 dwellings approved per 10,000 residents against a national median of 54). Nine views: the Accord tracker (national + per-state, monthly/rolling toggle), an SA3 choropleth across five measures with a skew-aware quantile ramp, a rankings leaderboard across six metrics, the signature Trajectory scatter (current supply intensity against three-year change, quadranted by medians, zoom/pan — the only form that separates a region that has always built a lot from one accelerating or collapsing), a Houses-vs-apartments view (100%-stacked national mix over time plus where each form actually gets approved), a States view with per-state small multiples and a state x building-type matrix, a searchable Explorer with rolling-12 sparklines, a click-through distribution histogram, and auto-detected insights — plus a hash-linkable per-region drill-down (#v=map&r=21304) with monthly house/apartment bars, value approved and rank. Dependency-free, unit-tested pipeline (its own SDMX CSV parser) that asserts the SA3 house + non-house last-12 split reproduces the total exactly and fails the build on drift; the one data subtlety is honest framing rather than a trap — the Accord target counts completions, not approvals, and the site labels the benchmark accordingly and notes that small-area SA3 detail lags the headline release by a few business days.

sites.name: au-unis
sites.description: Every Australian university joined into one interface from seven separate Department of Education workbooks — 42 institutions, 1,676,077 students, ten years of series, covering enrolments, international share, attrition, retention, subject success, completions, student-staff ratios and field mix. Two findings carry the site. First, the ATAR gradient: 93.7% of school leavers admitted with an ATAR of 95-100 complete a bachelor degree within nine years against 55.0% of those admitted at 30-49, a 38.7-point gap. Second, and the reason the signature view exists: the four-year completion rate everyone quotes (41.5%) is NOT the failure rate, because 35.5% of that cohort are still enrolled — plenty of degrees run longer than four years and part-time students longer again. Given nine years, 70.5% have completed. The 'Who finishes' view therefore defaults to nine years and teaches the caveat through its 4/6/9-year toggle: moving it visibly drains the grey 'still enrolled' band into the teal 'completed' band, so the user learns the trap by operating the control rather than reading a footnote. The other headline: 598,882 of 1,676,077 students (35.7%) have a permanent home residence outside Australia, a larger group than NSW and Victoria combined and the single largest origin in the country; Murdoch is 57.4% international, Sydney 50.8%, RMIT 50.0%. Eight views: rankings across 8 measures with the national median marked, the cohort-outcome decomposition sliced by ATAR/SES/disability/First Nations/regionality and 10 more attributes, a log-scaled exposure scatter quadranted by medians with zoom/pan and label de-collision that avoids both other labels and the dots themselves, the 9x10 origin-destination matrix as Sankey + choropleth + exact numbers, a squarified treemap plus institution x field heatmap, ten years annotated with the 2020 border closure and 2024 visa tightening, a sortable Explorer with sparklines, and auto-detected insights — plus a hash-linkable per-university drill-down (#i=3035). Built around EIGHT traps that each produce a confidently wrong number: (1) aggregate rows (National Total, Table A Providers, State Total, and a per-state Non-University Higher Education Institutions bucket) sit in the same column as real universities, so ranking them together counts the country several times; (2) np / '< 5' / '.' are string sentinels in numeric columns where Number(x)||0 gives a confident zero — a withheld cell is 1-4, never 0; (3) zeros in the historic rate series mean 'not a reporting provider yet' — Avondale reads 0 attrition for 2014-2022 then 12.65, and left alone ranks as the best-performing university in Australia; (4) sector attrition (domestic, transfers don't count as leaving) and provider attrition (overseas, transfers do) have different denominators and never share an axis; (5) the four-year completion trap above; (6) footnote markers and provider codes are welded into institution names inconsistently between workbooks, so the join key must be normalised or the same university appears twice; (7) the staff workbooks span headers over three merged rows with two metric blocks side by side; (8) footnote paragraphs are written into data columns in Section 17 and the time series. A ninth lives in the frontend: the interstate map excludes overseas students on purpose — include them and every state is an importer, so the map shades one uniform colour and the interstate story (Tasmania takes in domestic students at 1.47x, Queensland loses them at 0.87x) disappears entirely. The pipeline is dependency-free — its own minimal zip + xlsx reader, so CI never installs anything — and asserts its parsed national total reproduces the department's published 1,676,077 exactly, failing the build on drift. education.gov.au refuses bare fetch() clients and initially failed on CI with connect timeouts; fixed with full browser headers (incl. Sec-Fetch-*) plus dns ipv4first, since GitHub runners advertise IPv6 and the host only half-answers on it.
